chunks: Sa'd ibn Abdillah from al-Hasan ibn Ali from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf from some of our companions from al-Rida (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about the person in Ihram who has a sick companion, and he shaded his head; is it permissible for him to shade himself? He said: Yes. And it does not contradict the first report, because his saying 'Is it permissible for him to shade himself?' does not specify that it is for the sick person to shade himself. It is possible that the reference returns to the sick person, and the question was about that, whether it is permissible for him or not. He said: Yes.

key_terms.الْمُحْرِمِ: The person in the state of Ihram (ritual consecration)
key_terms.يَسْتَظِلَّ: To seek shade / to shade oneself

ai.seo_question: Can a person in Ihram shade a sick companion's head without breaking their Ihram?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records Imam al-Rida’s nuanced juristic reasoning (ijtihad) to resolve an apparent contradiction (ikhtilaf) in earlier reports regarding whether shading a sick companion invalidates the shadier’s Ihram. The Imam clarifies that the permission is context-dependent, demonstrating the Shia principle of reconciling narrations through precise linguistic analysis of the pronouns' referents. This highlights the importance of distinguishing between the act of shading for another versus shading for oneself in ritual law.
